# Programming with Python {.unnumbered}

> *"Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for
> machines to execute."* — @abelson1996, preface to the first edition.

This part corresponds to the first course of the master: an introduction to
programming in Python. It takes a reader who has never programmed to the point
of writing a small but well-structured application that stores its data in
files, handles errors gracefully, uses third-party packages in an isolated
environment — and can judge code written by an AI assistant.

The chapters follow the natural order in which the skills build on each other:
how computers and programs work; values and types; collections of data;
decisions and repetition; functions; classes and objects; errors; files;
organising code into modules and packages; the standard library; installing
packages; virtual environments; and, finally, AI tools for writing code.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this part matters for an AI engineer
Every later part of the book — data analysis, machine learning, deep learning,
reinforcement learning, generative AI — is written in Python. Structuring
programs, handling data and managing dependencies are the skills that turn a
computational idea into working, maintainable code.
:::

## What you will be able to do {.unnumbered}

1. Explain what a program and an algorithm are, and measure how the cost of an
   algorithm grows (@sec-ch-intro).
2. Store and transform data with Python's types, and present it neatly
   (@sec-ch-variables).
3. Pick the right collection for a job and know what each operation costs
   (@sec-ch-collections).
4. Write correct decisions with Boolean logic (@sec-ch-conditionals).
5. Write loops and convince yourself — or prove — that they are correct and
   terminate (@sec-ch-loops).
6. Break a problem into reusable functions (@sec-ch-functions).
7. Model entities with classes, special methods and inheritance (@sec-ch-oop).
8. Detect and handle errors instead of crashing (@sec-ch-exceptions).
9. Read and write text, CSV, JSON and binary files safely (@sec-ch-files).
10. Organise code into modules and installable packages (@sec-ch-modules).
11. Use the standard library for system, time and numeric tasks
    (@sec-ch-stdlib).
12. Install and pin third-party packages (@sec-ch-pip).
13. Create reproducible, isolated environments (@sec-ch-venv).
14. Use AI coding tools productively and verify what they produce
    (@sec-ch-ai-tools).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

None. You only need a computer with a web browser. Chapter
[-@sec-ch-intro] explains how to install Python or how to use it online.

## Map of the part {.unnumbered}

| Chapter | Core topics | What the book adds |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-ch-intro | programs, algorithms, the development environment | von Neumann model, binary numbers (with proofs), Euclid's algorithm, the halting problem, asymptotic notation, CPython and bytecode |
| @sec-ch-variables | input/output, variables, types, conversions, formatting | names vs objects, two's complement, IEEE 754 floating point with error bounds, Unicode and UTF-8, the format-spec mini-language |
| @sec-ch-collections | lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries | dynamic arrays and amortised analysis, hash tables and their expected cost, sorting and its lower bound, aliasing |
| @sec-ch-conditionals | Boolean expressions, `if`/`elif`/`else` | Boolean algebra, De Morgan's laws, short-circuit evaluation, truthiness, `match`, Böhm–Jacopini |
| @sec-ch-loops | `while`, `for`, `break`, `continue` | iteration protocol, induction, loop invariants, binary search, comprehensions |
| @sec-ch-functions | defining functions, arguments, return values | scope, closures, decorators, recursion and its cost, generators |
| @sec-ch-oop | classes, special methods, inheritance, polymorphism | class invariants, the laws of `__eq__`/`__lt__`, Liskov substitution, C3 linearisation, dataclasses |
| @sec-ch-exceptions | exceptions, `try`/`except`/`finally`, `raise`, `assert` | the exception hierarchy, chaining, EAFP vs LBYL, context managers |
| @sec-ch-files | text, binary, CSV, TSV, JSON files | encodings, the PNG format and CRC checksums, RFC 4180 and RFC 8259, atomic writes |
| @sec-ch-modules | modules and packages | the import system, information hiding, dependency graphs, `pyproject.toml` and wheels |
| @sec-ch-stdlib | `sys`, `os`, `time`, `datetime`, `math` | Unix time, calendar arithmetic, error of floating-point sums, `argparse` |
| @sec-ch-pip | PyPI, `pip`, versions, `requirements.txt` | PEP 440, semantic versioning, dependency resolution is NP-complete |
| @sec-ch-venv | virtual environments, Jupyter kernels, sharing projects | how `venv` works, lock files, conda and containers; NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib primer |
| @sec-ch-ai-tools | ChatGPT, Cursor, Copilot; vibe coding vs structured prompting | how LLMs generate code, temperature, the pass@$k$ estimator, a verification checklist |
| @sec-ch-project-phonebook | the final project | requirements, design, code review, tested reference implementation |

## The final project {.unnumbered}

The course ends with a **terminal phone-book prototype**: an interactive
console application, designed with object-oriented principles, that adds,
lists, edits, deletes and searches contacts, saves them to a JSON file, and
never crashes on wrong input. @sec-ch-project-phonebook states the
requirements in my own words, maps each of them to the chapters above, and
walks through the implementation published in
[`Phone_Book_Python_OOP.ipynb`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects/blob/main/Phone_Book_Python_OOP.ipynb).
